title: Efficient Analysis of Carrier Transport and TM-TE Emission in AlGaN UVC LEDs via Multi-band Localization Landscape Theory
authors: Yu-Ming Chang, Ping-Jie Zhuang, Marcel Filoche, Claude Weisbuch, James S. Speck, Yuh-Renn Wu
abstract: AlGaN-based UVC LEDs (220-250 nm) suffer from poor hole confinement and strain-induced |Z>-band dominance at high Al content (>60%), leading to increased TM emission and reduced external quantum efficiency (EQE). While conventional k.p models combined with Schrodinger, Poisson, and drift-diffusion solvers are widely used to study optical transitions, they are computationally expensive. In this work, we apply the multiband Localization Landscape (LL) model, including the effect of strain, as an alternative that replaces the eigenvalue problem to efficiently capture quantum effects and carrier localization. Using the 3D multi-band LL model with the Wigner-Weyl formalism, we reproduce emission and absorption spectra trends similar to the results in 3D k.p calculations, but with significantly reduced simulation time. The polarization ratio also agrees well with published experimental results across a wide spectral range. Furthermore, we analyze electrical characteristics such as band structure, polarization switching, and carrier confinement under alloy fluctuations and strain. This multi-band LL-based approach provides a fast and reliable solution for understanding and optimizing UVC LED performance.
summary: This paper introduces an efficient Multi-band Localization Landscape (LL) model to simulate carrier transport and emission in AlGaN UVC LEDs. By replacing computationally intensive k.p eigenvalue problems with the LL formalism, the authors achieve significant speedups while maintaining accuracy. The method successfully models complex physics like strain effects and polarization switching crucial for optimizing high-efficiency deep-UV light sources.
main_problem: The primary goal is to efficiently analyze carrier transport and determine TM-TE emission characteristics in AlGaN UVC LEDs, overcoming the computational expense of conventional k.p models.
main_result: A novel multi-band Localization Landscape (LL) model significantly reduces simulation time while accurately reproducing spectral trends and polarization ratios compared to full 3D k.p calculations.
method: The authors employ a hybrid approach combining the LL model with the Wigner–Weyl formalism, solving it within a 3D drift-diffusion framework on a Finite Element Mesh (FEM).
model_or_system: The system is AlGaN UVC LEDs. The methodology involves coupling the LL theory to solve for carrier localization and band structure changes induced by strain and alloy fluctuations, which are then fed into a 3D drift-diffusion solver.
key_observables: Emission/absorption spectra trends, polarization ratio (TE/TM), band structure, hole/electron current densities ($J_p, J_n$), and quantum efficiency (EQE).
important_parameters: Al composition ($	ext{Al}_x	ext{Ga}_{1-x}	ext{N}$), strain tensor components, operating wavelength (220–300 nm), and doping profiles.
main_assumptions: The LL theory is assumed to provide an accurate approximation of the full Schrödinger eigenvalue problem, allowing for computational efficiency gains. Strain effects are incorporated via deformation-potential terms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate band structure transitions based on polarization/strain, local strain variation causing band switching, and comparisons of carrier current density maps with and without including the crucial strain-induced deformation term.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical problem (UVC LEDs), details the limitations of existing k.p methods, proposes the LL model as an efficient alternative, validates it by comparing results to known physics (strain effects on hole transport), and concludes with analysis of device performance metrics like IQE.
why_interesting: The development of a computationally tractable quantum mechanical framework (LL model) that successfully replaces complex eigenvalue solvers for semiconductor device simulation is highly relevant to modeling open quantum systems in solid-state devices.
